title: How Compose works
scopeHtml: Scope: declarative model, the three phases, composable contract, compiler plugin, slot table, positional memoization and group keys, Recomposer and frame clock, Compose vs Views at runtime.

questions.promptHtml: What does "declarative UI" mean in Jetpack Compose, and how is it different from how you built screens with Views?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you think "UI = f(state)" or still think "find the view and mutate it". Everything else in Compose follows from this.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I describe what the UI looks like for the current state, and Compose figures out how to get there. With Views I held a tree of long-lived objects and mutated them (textView.text = ..., view.visibility = ...). In Compose the composable functions are re-run when the state they read changes, and the runtime updates only the parts of the tree that differ. State is the single source of truth, the UI is derived from it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Imperative Views: the tree is the state. You can get it out of sync with your model (forgot to hide the spinner on the error path). Declarative: the model is the state, the tree is a projection of it.

Views:    event -> findViewById -> setText/setVisibility ... (you diff by hand)
Compose:  event -> state change -> composables re-run -> runtime diffs -> LayoutNodes updated

Compose does not rebuild everything. A composable that read a changed State is invalidated and re-executed ("recomposed"). Output is not a tree of widgets returned to you; the function emits nodes/changes into the Composer (slot table). Inputs that did not change let Compose skip the function.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Counter(count: Int, onInc: () -> Unit) {
    // No "update the label" code anywhere. count changes -> this re-runs.
    Button(onClick = onInc) { Text("Clicked $count") }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "Compose redraws everything on each change". It re-executes only invalidated scopes, and the draw phase is separate.
  • Keeping UI state in a plain var (not snapshot state). Compose never learns it changed.
  • Thinking composables "return" UI. They return Unit and emit into the composition.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the state live? → Hoisted above, in a ViewModel or remember; composables are stateless where possible.
  2. Is Compose retained or immediate mode? → Retained-ish: a persistent node tree plus slot table, not a redraw-each-frame immediate mode.
  3. What triggers recomposition? → Writes to snapshot State objects read during composition (see the snapshot question later).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "state drives UI, no findViewById". Senior adds: the runtime keeps a slot table and node tree, invalidation is tracked per recompose scope via snapshot reads, and declarative does not mean "free": you still control what is read where.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams migrating from Views kept mirroring state in both a ViewModel and local vars, producing screens that show stale data after rotation. Single source of truth fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the three phases Compose goes through to produce a frame.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Phases are the base for every perf answer (deferred reads, graphicsLayer, lambda modifiers).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Composition decides what to show by running composables and building the tree. Layout measures and places each node. Drawing renders them to a canvas. Each phase can be skipped if its inputs did not change, and state read in a phase invalidates that phase (and later ones), not earlier ones.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
state write
   |
   v
Composition  -> runs composable functions, produces/updates LayoutNode tree
   |
Layout       -> measure (top-down constraints, bottom-up sizes), then place
   |
Drawing      -> DrawScope commands recorded into RenderNode display lists

Per the official docs, reads in composition invalidate composition and potentially later phases; reads in layout invalidate layout and draw; reads in draw invalidate draw only. This is why Modifier.offset { } or Modifier.graphicsLayer { } with a lambda can animate without any recomposition.

Layout itself has two steps: measure (parent gives constraints, child returns size) and place (parent positions children). Compose enforces single measurement per child per pass.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Box1(offsetPx: State<Int>) {
    Box(
        Modifier
            .offset { IntOffset(offsetPx.value, 0) } // read in layout phase
            .size(48.dp)
            .drawBehind { /* reads here hit draw only */ }
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Describing phases as "Compose, Measure, Draw" without saying what invalidates what.
  • Believing the phases always run together. They are independently skippable.
  • Reading scrollState.value directly in the composable body when only draw needs it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which phase does Modifier.offset(x = dp) vs offset { } read in? → Value form takes a value in composition; lambda form defers the state read to placement.
  2. Is there a phase before composition? → Conceptually the frame clock/snapshot apply; composition is first of the three.
  3. Can layout trigger recomposition? → Yes via SubcomposeLayout (e.g. LazyColumn, BoxWithConstraints) which composes during layout; also by writing state read earlier.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists phases. Senior states the invalidation rule per phase, names deferred-read modifiers, and mentions subcomposition breaking the clean ordering.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A parallax header read listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset in composition; recomposing 200 times per fling. Moving the read into graphicsLayer {} cut recomposition to zero.

questions.promptHtml: What is a composable function, and why should it be free of side effects and safe to call many times?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The composable contract (idempotent, side-effect free, any order, possibly skipped or cancelled) is what makes effects APIs necessary.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A composable is a function annotated @Composable that emits UI into the composition and can only be called from other composables. Compose may call it many times, skip it, run it on another thread in the future, in a different order, or abandon a run midway. So the body must be a pure description of UI from its inputs. Anything with side effects goes into effect handlers like LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect or SideEffect.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The official contract: composables are fast, idempotent, side-effect free, may run in any order, may run in parallel (not default yet), and recomposition can be cancelled and restarted. Therefore:

  • A second call with the same input must give the same emitted output.
  • Writing to a shared list or logging analytics in the body runs on every recomposition, including ones discarded.
  • Because recomposition can skip, you cannot rely on a body "running at least once per change" for non-UI work.

@Composable is not just an annotation; the compiler plugin rewrites the signature (adds Composer, $changed) so a composable can only be called with a Composer in scope. That is why you cannot call one from a click listener.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: side effect in body
@Composable
fun Screen(vm: VM) {
    vm.trackView()            // runs on every recomposition
    Text("Hi")
}

// Correct
@Composable
fun ScreenOk(vm: VM) {
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) { vm.trackView() } // once per entering composition
    Text("Hi")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mutating a non-state collection in the body (items.add(...)).
  • Assuming println in the body shows how many times "the screen" updated; it shows scope executions.
  • Calling suspend functions or starting coroutines directly in the body.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can't I call a composable from onClick? → No Composer in that scope; onClick is a plain lambda, not a composable one.
  2. SideEffect vs LaunchedEffect? → SideEffect runs after every successful recomposition, non-suspending; LaunchedEffect runs a coroutine keyed on its keys.
  3. Can composables run in parallel? → The contract allows it; today recomposition runs on the main thread by default, so don't rely on either.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "no side effects in composables". Senior ties it to the compiler rewrite, skipping, cancelled recompositions, and concretely names which effect API replaces which pattern.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Double-counted impressions: analytics call in the body fired 3x on a scroll because of recomposition; moved to LaunchedEffect(item.id).

questions.promptHtml: If I read the same State<Float> in composition versus inside a graphicsLayer {} lambda, what exactly differs at runtime?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that snapshot reads are attributed to whichever observer is active (recompose scope vs layout/draw observers).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Reads are tracked by the snapshot system and attributed to the current observer. In the composable body, the observer is the recompose scope, so a change schedules recomposition of that scope. Inside a graphicsLayer {} lambda, the observer is the layer's invalidation, so only the draw/layer update runs and composition and layout are skipped.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Compose installs a read observer when executing a composition scope, when running layout (OwnerSnapshotObserver for measure/layout blocks), and when running draw/layer blocks. When a State is read, readObserver records (state -> scope). A later write sends an apply notification; each registered observer invalidates its own thing.

read in body        -> RecomposeScope.invalidate()      -> comp + layout + draw
read in layout lambda (offset { }) -> remeasure/relayout request -> layout + draw
read in graphicsLayer {} / drawBehind {} -> layer/draw invalidation -> draw only

Cost difference per frame: a composition is full function execution plus diff of its subtree; a draw invalidation just re-records display list for one layer.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Fade(alpha: State<Float>) {
    // Bad: reads in composition, recomposes every frame of animation
    Box(Modifier.alpha(alpha.value).size(100.dp))

    // Good: deferred read, draw/layer phase only
    Box(Modifier.graphicsLayer { this.alpha = alpha.value }.size(100.dp))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing state.value as a parameter down: the read happens in the parent's scope.
  • Assuming by delegate hides the read; it does not, val x by state reads when x is accessed.
  • Thinking derivedStateOf defers phases; it only reduces notifications.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you pass a deferred value to a child? → Pass () -> Float or State<Float>, read it in the lambda modifier.
  2. What does Layout Inspector show? → Recomposition counts: the deferred version stays at 0 while the other climbs.
  3. Does Modifier.offset { } skip layout too? → No, it re-runs layout/placement, skipping composition only.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior explains observer attribution and shows lambda-passing across component boundaries instead of values.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Animated progress bar recomposed its entire card at 60 fps; passing a () -> Float brought Layout Inspector counts to 0.

questions.contextHtml:
A collapsing toolbar was implemented as below. On a Pixel 6a the list scrolls at ~45 fps with p95 frame time 31 ms; JankStats reports 22% janky frames during scroll. Layout Inspector shows CollapsingHeader recomposition count rising by ~1 per frame while scrolling. Release build, baseline profile installed. The team suspects the images in the header are too big.

@Composable
fun CollapsingHeader(listState: LazyListState) {
    val offset = listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset
    val alpha = (1f - offset / 400f).coerceIn(0f, 1f)
    Column(Modifier.alpha(alpha)) {
        HeaderImage()
        TitleRow()
        ActionButtons()
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Downscale images / use remember." remember does not help because the input actually changes every frame, and the image red herring ignores the recomposition-per-frame signal.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is jank only in this screen (isolates cause)? Is the header content static? Which Compose version/strong skipping on? Does it janks on the first scroll only (image decode) or continuously?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the read to a deferred phase; a small diff that can hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) state read in composition causes per-frame recomposition of the entire header, (b) image decode, (c) overdraw, (d) alpha() modifier creating a layer.
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector recomposition counts (rising per frame confirms a), System Trace to see Recomposer:recompose slices each frame, compiler reports to see whether HeaderImage is skippable, Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric before/after.
  5. Root cause: firstVisibleItemScrollOffset is read in the composition body, so the scope is invalidated on every scroll delta; the whole Column subtree is re-executed each frame, on the main thread, just before layout.
  6. Fix: Short-term: Modifier.graphicsLayer { alpha = (1f - listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset / 400f).coerceIn(0f, 1f) } so the read is in the layer block. Long-term: a shared scroll-driven state holder exposing () -> Float.
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark scroll test in CI with a frame-timing threshold; review rule "scroll/animation values only read in lambda modifiers".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not derivedStateOf alone (still notifies in composition). Not downscaling images first; the data says the problem is recomposition. Note graphicsLayer alpha < 1 may allocate an offscreen layer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the title text must change at offset > 200? → Use derivedStateOf { offset > 200 } read in composition; it only invalidates on threshold crossing.
  • What if you also need height shrink? → Modifier.layout or offset { } reading the state in layout phase.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shopping app's sticky filter bar dropped to 40 fps; the cause was a single scrollState.value in a parent. Fix was a three-line move into graphicsLayer.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames images or adds remember.
  • Hire: identifies composition read, defers via lambda.
  • Strong hire: also verifies with traces, discusses derivedStateOf threshold pattern, offscreen-layer cost and CI benchmark.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between initial composition, recomposition, and a composition being disposed?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Lifecycle vocabulary underlies effects, remember, and bugs where state "resets".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Initial composition is the first run of the content, which builds the slot table and creates nodes. Recomposition re-runs only invalidated scopes against the existing slot table, updating what changed. Disposal happens when the composable leaves the composition (or the whole composition is disposed): remembered objects get onForgotten, effects get cancelled/disposed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
setContent {}           -> Composition created, Recomposer registers it
initial composition     -> every group inserted; remember{} calc executed; effects scheduled
state write             -> scopes invalidated -> recomposition (reads slot table, compares, updates)
node leaves (if/else)   -> group removed -> RememberObserver.onForgotten, DisposableEffect.onDispose
composition.dispose()   -> everything above for the whole tree

Recomposition is incremental: Composer walks the slot table, and for unchanged groups with skippable inputs it jumps over them (skipToGroupEnd). A "composable leaves" event is a removal from the slot table, not simply "not visible".

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Host(show: Boolean) {
    if (show) Detail() // false -> true is initial composition of Detail; true -> false disposes it
}

@Composable
fun Detail() {
    val obj = remember { Expensive() }   // new instance after each re-entry
    DisposableEffect(Unit) { onDispose { obj.close() } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying remember survives recomposition and configuration change. Only rememberSaveable handles config change.
  • Confusing "recomposition" with "re-entering": toggling show creates a new instance of Detail's state.
  • Treating a LazyColumn item scrolling off as disposal; it is, items are disposed (reuse pool keyed by content type).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What survives config change? → ViewModel and rememberSaveable; the Activity is recreated so the composition is rebuilt.
  2. Does LaunchedEffect restart on recomposition? → Only when keys change.
  3. Does RememberObserver.onRemembered run immediately? → It's dispatched after the composition is applied (post-apply), not during composition.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior knows effects/remember callbacks fire at apply time and that disposal is slot-table removal.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A video player in a LazyColumn re-initialized every scroll because the player lived in remember; hoisting it into a pooled holder fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: What does the Compose compiler plugin do to a @Composable function? What does the compiled signature look like?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows you know Compose is language-level plus runtime, not "just a library".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The plugin rewrites each composable: it adds a hidden Composer parameter and $changed bitmask parameters, wraps the body in startRestartGroup/endRestartGroup so it becomes a recompose scope, generates group keys from source location, and emits skip logic comparing parameters to previously stored ones. Defaults get a $default mask.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Conceptual output of:

@Composable fun Greeting(name: String) { Text(name) }
// Decompiled shape, simplified
fun Greeting(name: String, $composer: Composer?, $changed: Int) {
    $composer.startRestartGroup(<key>)
    val $dirty = $changed
    if ($changed and 0b0110 == 0) $dirty = $dirty or (if ($composer.changed(name)) 0b0100 else 0b0010)
    if ($dirty and 0b0011 != 0b0010 || !$composer.skipping) {
        Text(name, $composer, 0)
    } else {
        $composer.skipToGroupEnd()
    }
    $composer.endRestartGroup()?.updateScope { c, _ -> Greeting(name, c, $changed or 1) }
}

Key points:

  • $changed packs per-parameter state (roughly: uncertain / same / different / static) in a few bits each, so parents can tell children "this arg is a known constant, no comparison needed". Exact bit layout is a compiler implementation detail; do not rely on it.
  • updateScope registers the lambda used to re-run just this function on invalidation (restartable).
  • Calls to composables from a composable get their own groups; control flow (if, loops) is wrapped in groups (startReplaceGroup / movable groups) so identity is positional.
  • Compose compiler lives in the Kotlin repo since Kotlin 2.0 (Gradle plugin org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose); before that it was a separate artifact with a Kotlin version pin.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
(compiler metrics to inspect)

// build.gradle.kts
composeCompiler {
    reportsDestination = layout.buildDirectory.dir("compose_reports")
    metricsDestination = layout.buildDirectory.dir("compose_metrics")
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "annotation processing". It is a Kotlin compiler (IR) plugin.
  • Claiming the whole function body re-runs always. Skippable ones may skip.
  • Claiming @Composable lambdas are not transformed; they are too (composable lambda with composableLambda caching).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the Compose compiler version used to be tied to Kotlin? → It uses unstable compiler internals; Kotlin 2.0 moved it in-tree.
  2. What makes a function restartable but not skippable? → Unstable params before strong skipping, or non-Unit return; it can still be re-run as its own scope.
  3. What is $default? → A bitmask telling the callee which default-value expressions to evaluate inside the function.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior can sketch the decompiled shape, explain $changed, and relate it to stability reports.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Debugging a mysterious perf regression after a Kotlin bump: reports showed several screens' composables flipped from skippable to non-skippable.

questions.contextHtml:
QA reports the "Recently viewed" count badge sometimes shows 2x or 3x the real number after scrolling a feed of 5,000 items; it also differs between debug and release builds. Crash-free is unaffected (99.8%). The code:

@Composable
fun FeedItem(item: Item, viewed: MutableList<String>) {
    if (!viewed.contains(item.id)) viewed.add(item.id)
    Text(item.title)
}
// parent: val viewed = remember { mutableListOf<String>() }
// badge:  Text("${viewed.size}")

A teammate thinks it's a threading bug and wants to wrap it in synchronized.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose this and propose the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the list thread-safe". The list is only touched on main; the real issue is the contract.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should "viewed" mean "was composed" or "was actually visible for N ms"? Is it persisted? Does duplicate id counting happen (it should not)? Which screens use it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop writing from the body; disable badge increment via remote flag if needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) side effect in composition, (b) non-observable list so the badge is stale/inconsistent, (c) threading, (d) key collisions.
  4. How I'd verify: Log in the body with a counter; Layout Inspector recomposition counts; run with a test that recomposes via composeTestRule and checks mutation; note LazyColumn prefetch composes off-screen items.
  5. Root cause: Composition is not a "visible" event. LazyColumn prefetches/composes items that are never shown, and items are disposed and recomposed on scroll back. The body mutates a plain list that Compose does not observe, so the badge text is not even invalidated reliably; it shows whatever size existed at its own last recomposition.
  6. Fix: Short-term: remove mutation from the body; report views in LaunchedEffect(item.id) { onViewed(item.id) } (still means "entered composition"). Long-term: use a visibility signal from LazyListState.layoutInfo via snapshotFlow with a debounce into the ViewModel, which owns a Set, exposing it as StateFlow.
  7. Prevention: Lint/review rule: no writes to non-state in composable bodies; tests using ComposeTestRule that recompose twice.
  8. Trade-offs: synchronized hides the bug; dedupe via a Set alone still counts prefetched items.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if product says "viewed = 50% visible for 1s"? → snapshotFlow on layoutInfo + distinctUntilChanged + a timer per item in the ViewModel.
  • Why does release differ from debug? → Different prefetch/timing and recomposition counts; the contract never promised a count.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Analytics undercounted by 30% after a Compose migration because impression logging lived in the body and skipping removed calls.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds locks.
  • Hire: moves to effect and explains why body runs are not events.
  • Strong hire: proposes visible-for-N-ms pipeline with snapshotFlow and discusses prefetch.

questions.promptHtml: What is the slot table, and what does "positional memoization" mean?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: remember, keys, and "why did my state move to the wrong item" all reduce to this.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The slot table is the runtime's memory of a composition: a flat, gap-buffer-backed array structure storing groups (with keys) and the values stored in them (remembered objects, parameters, nodes). Positional memoization means a composable call's identity is its position in the call tree, so remember finds its value by "I am the Nth slot inside this group at this call site", not by a name.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the AndroidX design notes, the slot table arrays act as a gap buffer when written: edits (insert/delete/move of groups) are cheap near the gap, and sequential execution during recomposition matches that access pattern. Group indices ignore the gap; anchors keep stable positions for scopes to find themselves.

slot table (conceptual)
[G key=A | slots: param, remember-value ... | [G key=B | ...] [G key=C | ...] ]  <gap>

On recomposition the Composer replays the same call sequence reading from the table: at each startGroup(key) it checks whether the next group has the same key. Same -> reuse its slots (this is how remember returns the old object). Different -> insert/skip/remove or look ahead to find a moved group.

Compose never compares trees the way a virtual DOM does; it uses call order and keys as the identity.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Row2() {
    val a = remember { Counter() }  // slot 0 in this group
    val b = remember { Counter() }  // slot 1; identity = position
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Describing slot table as a "tree of views".
  • Saying remember uses a name/key from the variable. It is purely positional (plus explicit key params).
  • Claiming it is a hash map.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a gap buffer? → Edits cluster at the current execution point; moving the gap is cheaper than shifting on each change. Treat any specific complexity claims as approximate.
  2. What happens when conditionals change the call order? → Different groups are inserted/removed; state in removed ones is forgotten.
  3. Where are nodes stored? → Node references live in the slot table too; the applier mutates the actual LayoutNode tree.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior connects it to key(), movable content, and the invalidation anchors, and knows it is not a diff.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: State appearing on the wrong list row after reorder, traced to positional identity with no keys.

questions.promptHtml: How do compiler-generated keys and the explicit key() composable interact, and when do you need key?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Identity bugs in lists are one of the most common real Compose bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The compiler gives each call site a static group key from its source position, so different call sites are distinguishable. But a loop emits the same call site repeatedly, so identity falls back to order. key(id) { } adds a dynamic key so Compose can match a group across reorderings and keep its remembered state and effects with the right item. LazyColumn's items(key = ) serves the same role.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without keys, for items.forEach { Row(it) } the groups are in the order [Row, Row, Row]. If the list reorders, Compose matches by position: row 0's state stays at position 0 while the data for it changes. Parameters get updated, but remembered state (scroll, text field input, animation) remains at the position. With key(item.id) the Composer looks up the group by key and moves it, preserving state.

Keys must be unique among siblings and stable; duplicates crash in Lazy lists ("Key was already used") and degrade silently elsewhere. For LazyColumn, a key also makes rememberSaveable state survive, as state is saved against the key (it must be Bundle-able).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Todos(items: List<Todo>) {
    Column {
        items.forEach { todo ->
            key(todo.id) {           // identity follows the id, not the index
                TodoRow(todo)        // owns remember { } state
            }
        }
    }
}

LazyColumn {
    items(items, key = { it.id }) { TodoRow(it) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using index as key (equivalent to no key under reorder).
  • Using non-unique keys, or keys like hashCode() that collide.
  • Adding key for if/else branches; use separate call sites or movableContentOf instead.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. key vs contentType? → Key is identity; contentType allows reuse of compositions between different items of the same type.
  2. What happens when a key changes for the same row? → Treated as remove + insert; state is lost.
  3. How do you move a stateful composable between parents? → movableContentOf.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions static vs dynamic keys, stable ids (not indices), duplicate key crashes, and movableContentOf.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Drag-to-reorder list kept each row's expanded state at the old index until stable ids were used.

questions.contextHtml:
A chat list of ~300 messages gets new messages inserted at the top (index 0) via websocket. Users report: when a new message arrives, the text they were typing in an inline "reply" field on message #3 jumps to a different message, and a "like" animation replays on the wrong bubble. Crash rate is 0%. Code:

@Composable
fun Chat(messages: List<Message>) {
    LazyColumn {
        itemsIndexed(messages) { index, msg ->
            MessageRow(msg)   // contains remember { mutableStateOf("") } for the reply text
        }
    }
}

A teammate proposes switching to Column + verticalScroll "so state is simpler".
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and what is your fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use rememberSaveable". Saveable state is still keyed by position/key; without a key it keeps the same wrong slot.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do messages have stable unique ids server-side? Are messages ever edited/replaced (id change)? Is pagination appending at the end or top?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a key using the server message id.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) no key so identity is position in LazyColumn, (b) remember state per slot not per message, (c) animation state tied to slot, (d) not an issue with Column swap (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify: Reproduce with a test inserting at index 0; log remember initial creation with item id; Layout Inspector.
  5. Root cause: itemsIndexed without key defaults key to the index. Inserting at 0 shifts all data by one index while item N keeps slot-state of index N; so the typed text stays at index 3 but now shows next to different data.
  6. Fix: items(messages, key = { it.id }, contentType = { it.type }). Long-term, hoist reply drafts into a Map<MessageId, String> in the ViewModel.
  7. Prevention: Lint check (Compose lint warns about missing keys in some cases; verify per version) plus a UI test that inserts at the head.
  8. Trade-offs: Column with 300 items composes all of them (no laziness); that would hurt more than help.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if ids may repeat across pages? → Compose key must be unique; use "${page}:${id}" or dedupe at the repository.
  • Does a key affect scroll position on insertion? → Yes, with keys the list can keep the first visible item anchored by key.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A support inbox showed "typing" indicators on the wrong ticket after websocket inserts; the cause was index keys.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swaps container or uses saveable.
  • Hire: stable key with id.
  • Strong hire: also hoists draft state, handles duplicate ids, uses contentType, understands scroll anchoring.

questions.promptHtml: What do "restartable" and "skippable" mean for a composable, and how does $changed enable skipping?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who memorized "use stable types" from people who understand the mechanism.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Restartable means the compiler wrapped the function in a restart group, so when state it read changes, Compose can re-run just that function. Skippable means that on a parent-triggered recomposition, if all parameters are known to be the same as last time, the body is skipped. Same-ness is determined by $changed (what the caller already knows) plus equality checks against stored parameter values.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Restartable: has endRestartGroup()?.updateScope. Almost all composables returning Unit.
  • Skippable: the compiler generates the parameter comparison and skipToGroupEnd. Before strong skipping, a function was skippable only when all parameters were stable. Inline functions and functions returning a value are not restartable/skippable.
  • With strong skipping (default since Kotlin 2.0.20 per Android docs), functions with unstable parameters become skippable too, comparing unstable params by instance (===) and stable ones by equals(); lambdas capturing unstable values are remembered.
  • A call can be skipped without any comparison when $changed says static/same (a literal argument).
parent recomposes -> calls Child(a, b, $changed=…)
  Child: for each param: caller says "same"? yes -> trust. unknown? -> composer.changed(a)
  all same + not forced -> skipToGroupEnd()  (body not run)

Invalidation by own state read still re-runs the body regardless of parameter equality (that is the restart path).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Title(text: String, onClick: () -> Unit) { /* skippable if text same and onClick same */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking skippable means "never recomposes". A state read inside forces a restart.
  • Assuming strong skipping makes stability irrelevant; instance equality for unstable types fails when you create a new instance each time.
  • Believing remembered lambdas are required in all cases (strong skipping memoizes them).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you check? → Compiler reports composables.txt ("restartable skippable").
  2. What makes a function non-restartable? → inline, or returns a non-Unit value (they are not restartable groups).
  3. What if there are 40 parameters? → $changed is Int-wide per ~10 parameters, additional $changedN ints are added (verify bit counts per compiler version).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior cites strong-skipping semantics with the Kotlin version, distinguishes restart from skip, and describes verification with reports.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An upgrade to Kotlin 2.0.20 reduced list recomposition by double digits without code change because strong skipping was default-on.

questions.promptHtml: Who actually triggers recomposition, and when? Explain the Recomposer and the frame clock.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of timing: why multiple state writes coalesce, why animations in effects use withFrameNanos, and why recomposition is main-thread work in a frame.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: State writes are recorded in the snapshot system. When a snapshot applies, observers are notified, scopes that read the changed state are invalidated, and the Recomposer is told it has work. The Recomposer runs a coroutine loop that waits for a frame from a MonotonicFrameClock (on Android backed by the Choreographer), then recomposes all invalidated compositions in one batch and applies changes. Many writes in a frame collapse into one recomposition.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
state.value = x  --> global snapshot write
Snapshot.sendApplyNotifications()  (scheduled via a global-write observer)
   --> Recomposer.recordComposerModifications(): collect invalidated scopes
   --> Recomposer.runRecomposeAndApplyChanges loop:
         awaitWorkAvailable -> parentFrameClock.withFrameNanos { frameTime ->
              broadcastFrameClock.sendFrame(frameTime)   // animations/withFrameNanos callers
              recompose invalidated compositions
              applyChanges (nodes, remember observers, effects)
         }
Choreographer frame callback -> input/animation -> traversals (measure/layout/draw)
  • On Android the clock is AndroidUiFrameClock wrapping Choreographer; withFrameNanos suspends until next frame. (Docs: the Recomposer can pause broadcast of the frame clock during recomposition, delaying animation callbacks.)
  • Recomposer is created per window by the platform (WindowRecomposerFactory) in the Android integration; its effect context uses the main dispatcher.
  • Changes are applied (applyChanges) after composition; SideEffect, LaunchedEffect launches, and onRemembered callbacks run then.
  • Recomposition during a frame that writes state again triggers another pass in the same frame loop or next frame; unbounded loops cause the "recomposition storm".

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
    while (true) {
        withFrameNanos { frameTime -> progress = (frameTime / 1_000_000L % 1000) / 1000f }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying each state write recomposes immediately.
  • Claiming Compose has its own render thread; composition and layout happen on the main thread, draw records on main and renders on RenderThread.
  • Forgetting that effects run after apply, not during composition.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if two writes occur in one frame? → One recomposition; last write wins.
  2. What dispatcher does LaunchedEffect use? → The composition's coroutine context (AndroidUiDispatcher, main) with the frame clock.
  3. Why is LaunchedEffect with delay loop worse than withFrameNanos for animation? → It is not frame-aligned and can drop or double frames.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior can narrate from write to Choreographer, mention batching, apply phase ordering, and the interaction between frame clock and tests (mainClock.autoAdvance).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An animation using delay(16) stuttered under load; swapping to withFrameNanos aligned it to vsync.

questions.promptHtml: How does Compose attach to an Android Activity? What is AndroidComposeView and what does setContent do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Interop and lifecycle bugs (ComposeView in Fragments, RecyclerView items) need this model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: setContent creates (or finds) a ComposeView in the Activity's content view; when attached to a window it creates an AndroidComposeView, a regular ViewGroup that is the bridge: it owns the root LayoutNode tree, handles measure/layout/draw/input dispatch from the Android view system, and hosts a Composition driven by the window's Recomposer. So Compose lives inside the View hierarchy; to the platform it is one View.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Activity.setContent { }  (ComponentActivity ext)
   -> ComposeView(this).apply { setContent }  added to android.R.id.content
ComposeView (AbstractComposeView)
   -> on attach: ensure window Recomposer + ViewTreeLifecycleOwner/SavedStateRegistryOwner
   -> creates AndroidComposeView (owner of root LayoutNode), and a Composition with its content
Android measure/layout/draw  -> AndroidComposeView.onMeasure/onLayout/dispatchDraw -> LayoutNodes
touch events -> AndroidComposeView.dispatchTouchEvent -> pointer input system

ComposeView requires owners (Lifecycle, SavedState) found on the view tree; in Fragments/RecyclerView they must be provided (Fragment does this). ViewCompositionStrategy controls disposal: default (verify per release) is DisposeOnDetachedFromWindowOrReleasedFromPool; use DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed for Fragments.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Fragment
override fun onCreateView(i: LayoutInflater, c: ViewGroup?, s: Bundle?) =
    ComposeView(requireContext()).apply {
        setViewCompositionStrategy(
            ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed
        )
        setContent { MaterialTheme { Screen() } }
    }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming Compose bypasses the View system. Window, input, and rendering still go through ViewRootImpl and the RenderThread.
  • Using the default strategy in a Fragment with back stack: composition disposed on detach while the Fragment's view is retained, losing remember state.
  • Forgetting multiple ComposeViews each have their own Composition (sharing the window Recomposer).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Cost of many ComposeViews in a RecyclerView? → Each is a separate composition; creation is expensive, so use pooling strategy and keep few per screen.
  2. How does CompositionLocal reach children? → Provided at the root of the composition (ProvideAndroidCompositionLocals: Context, Configuration, LifecycleOwner, etc.).
  3. How does Compose get the Recomposer? → WindowRecomposerPolicy creates one per window root, tied to the window lifecycle.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior mentions ViewTree owners, strategies and per-ComposeView composition cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Fragment screens lost state when navigating back until the composition strategy was changed.

questions.contextHtml:
A hybrid app embeds a ComposeView as the item view of a RecyclerView with 120 rows (profile cards). After the Compose rollout to 100% (400k DAU, mid-tier devices 3 GB RAM), Play vitals shows jank up 3x on this screen (p95 frame 48 ms) and OOM-related crash rate rose from 0.3% to 0.9%. LeakCanary on the debug build shows retained ComposeView instances after leaving the screen. Stack excerpt from a tester: IllegalStateException: ViewTreeLifecycleOwner not found from ...ComposeView. The item code:

class CardVH(parent: ViewGroup) : RecyclerView.ViewHolder(ComposeView(parent.context)) {
    fun bind(c: Card) { (itemView as ComposeView).setContent { CardUi(c) } }
}
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compose is just slower in lists; go back to Views." Misses setContent per bind and strategy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it the debug or release data? How many ComposeViews on screen (visible ~8)? Is the RecyclerView in a Fragment? Is setContent called on every bind?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature-flag back to the Views card for this screen if the crash rate is above budget; ship a hotfix with the strategy fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) setContent on every bind creates a new Composition each time while the old one may not be disposed until detach, (b) wrong ViewCompositionStrategy for RecyclerView/Fragment so compositions leak or die early, (c) heavy cards without keys/content type, (d) image sizes (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify: LeakCanary retained trace, System Trace to see composition creation (Compose:setContent) during scroll, Macrobenchmark scroll frame timing, heap dump counting Composition/Recomposer objects.
  5. Root cause: Each setContent call allocates a new Composition and subscribes it; ViewHolder reuse called it repeatedly. The default strategy disposes on window detach, but items offscreen but still attached/cached in the pool keep compositions alive, and the lifecycle owner lookup fails when the RecyclerView sits in a Fragment view hierarchy without owners set.
  6. Fix: Use ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed or the pool-aware default on a modern version (verify), call setContent once in the ViewHolder constructor and push data via a mutableStateOf held by the holder, set the owner via the Fragment's viewLifecycleOwner. Long-term: make the screen a single Compose LazyColumn.
  7. Prevention: LeakCanary in CI instrumentation, macrobenchmark guard on the screen, review rule for ComposeView in RecyclerView.
  8. Trade-offs: Pool-based holders cost memory; a full LazyColumn migration costs time but removes per-item compositions.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if each row is tiny? → Per-row ComposeView overhead dominates; prefer one ComposeView for the screen.
  • Does RecyclerView.RecycledViewPool help? → Reuses holders but not compositions' cost unless strategy supports release-from-pool.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "gradual Compose adoption" screen was slower than the Views version until the item ComposeViews were collapsed into one.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames Compose generally.
  • Hire: identifies per-bind setContent and strategy.
  • Strong hire: gives state-holder-per-holder pattern, lifecycle owners, and migration plan with measured gates.

questions.promptHtml: Compare Compose and the View system at runtime: invalidation, measurement, and what each costs per frame.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers must reason about when Compose is cheaper or costlier than Views, not repeat marketing.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Views invalidate whole subtrees by rect and re-run measure/layout/draw over View objects; nested layouts can measure children multiple times, which makes cost grow with depth. Compose tracks state reads per scope, skips what did not change, and enforces single-pass measurement per child, with intrinsics as the explicit escape hatch. Compose pays other costs: composition work on the main thread and slot-table bookkeeping, plus first-run class loading and JIT without baseline profiles.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect Views Compose
Update trigger You call setX/invalidate/requestLayout Snapshot state write -> scope invalidation
Granularity View (and ancestors on requestLayout) Recompose scope, then layout node/draw layer
Measure measure may run several times (e.g. weighted LinearLayout, RelativeLayout 2 passes) Each child measured once per pass; second measure throws; intrinsics for pre-queries
Tree objects Heavy View objects, XML inflation Lightweight LayoutNodes created by Applier; no inflation
Draw Display list per View, invalidate dirty rect Layers via graphicsLayer/RenderNode; draw phase can run alone
Startup Inflater, resources Class loading, JIT; mitigated by baseline profiles
Cost of deep nesting Nested weights can be exponential Linear because single-pass measure

Compose is not automatically faster: a poorly scoped state read can recompose a large subtree 60 times per second, while a Views TextView.setText touches one node. Debug builds make Compose look slower (no R8, no baseline profile, extra tooling), so benchmark release builds only.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Intrinsics: explicit way to ask a child "how big would you be?" before real measure
Row(Modifier.height(IntrinsicSize.Min)) {
    Text("A")
    VerticalDivider() // fills height of tallest sibling
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Compose is faster." It depends; measure release with Macrobenchmark.
  • Believing there is no requestLayout analog; layout invalidation exists and propagates via parent data/Modifier.layout.
  • Forgetting interop: AndroidView inside Compose has Views' costs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does measuring twice throw? → Enforces linear-time layout; use SubcomposeLayout or intrinsics.
  2. Where does Compose's startup cost come from? → Class loading/JIT in the first composition; baseline profiles reduce it.
  3. APK/dex size impact? → Compose adds runtime and library methods; R8 shrinks; verify with the build analyzer.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior balances claims, cites Compose's costs, and ties benchmarking to release builds with baseline profiles.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "Compose is slow" ticket evaporated when measured on a release build with a baseline profile.

questions.contextHtml: You own a 1.2M-DAU shopping app with 80 XML screens. Leadership wants "full Compose by Q4". Crash-free is 99.6%, cold start p50 is 1.4 s, p95 is 3.1 s on low-end devices (2 GB RAM, 25% of users). A pilot of the product-detail screen in Compose in a 5% experiment shows: cold start +180 ms p95, scroll jank flat, crash rate -0.1%, conversion neutral. A senior peer says "Compose will be strictly faster."
questions.promptHtml: How do you plan the migration and respond to the pilot results?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite all screens now; Compose is the future." Ignores data, rollout risk, and startup.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the +180 ms in the first Compose screen only (one-time class load) or every screen? Is the baseline profile shipped in the experiment build? Which devices regress? What is the startup budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the experiment at 5% on non-critical paths; do not put Compose in the launch path until the cost is understood.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) missing baseline profile (JIT/class load on first composition), (b) first ComposeView creation initialises Recomposer/Choreographer plumbing, (c) heavy initial composition with unkeyed lists, (d) Material3 theme setup.
  4. How I'd verify: Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric with and without baseline profile; Perfetto trace on a low-end device; compare Compose:setContent slices; Play vitals split by device class.
  5. Root cause (likely): first-use class loading and interpreted code without a baseline profile.
  6. Fix: Ship Compose baseline profile (generated for the Compose screens), enable R8 full mode, avoid Compose on the launch screen until the profile closes the gap, then migrate by leaf screens with ComposeView/AndroidView interop.
  7. Prevention: Startup and frame-timing benchmarks as release gates; a per-screen migration checklist; flags with a kill switch.
  8. Trade-offs: Mixed Views/Compose longer-term increases APK size and theme duplication; "big bang" rewrite risks regression and blocks feature work.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the budget is zero regression? → Migrate only screens off the launch path first; defer launch screens.
  • How do you prove "faster"? → Per-screen paired experiments on jank and startup, not intuition.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration looked 8% slower to start in staging because the benchmark ran a debug-signed build without profiles; the real fix was shipping the profile.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: all-in rewrite or reject Compose.
  • Hire: incremental plan with experiment and baseline profile.
  • Strong hire: quantifies budget, device split, gates, kill switch, interop cost.

questions.promptHtml: How does the snapshot system make mutableStateOf reads trigger recomposition? What are snapshots, and what is different about a write inside a composition?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The mechanism behind all "why did/didn't this recompose" questions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Snapshot state is multi-version: each State holds a linked list of records tagged with snapshot ids. Compose runs composition inside a mutable snapshot with a read observer that records which scope read which state. Writes mark the state modified; when the snapshot applies (or the global snapshot is advanced), apply observers fire and the Recomposer invalidates the scopes that read it. Isolation means a recomposition sees a consistent view of state.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Recomposer: val snap = Snapshot.takeMutableSnapshot(readObserver, writeObserver)
 snap.enter { composition.recompose() }       // reads recorded per RecomposeScope
 snap.apply()                                  // publish writes -> apply notifications
state.value = 1 (outside)  -> global snapshot write -> Snapshot.sendApplyNotifications()
   -> registered apply observer -> Recomposer finds scopes observing 'state' -> invalidate
  • Equality: mutableStateOf uses structuralEqualityPolicy() by default, so writing an equal value does not notify.
  • Mutable objects inside state (MutableList in mutableStateOf) are not tracked; use mutableStateListOf or immutable replacement.
  • Writing state that was already read earlier in the same composition triggers a second recomposition ("backwards write"); a loop of these is a recomposition storm.
  • derivedStateOf is a state whose dependencies are tracked; it notifies readers only when its computed result changes by its equality policy.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
var items by mutableStateOf(listOf<String>())   // replace list: tracked
val bad = mutableStateOf(mutableListOf<String>())
bad.value.add("x")                              // NOT tracked: same list instance

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mutating collection inside state.
  • Reading state in a ViewModel thread without a snapshot (reads are fine, writes are thread-safe but notifications are applied via the global snapshot).
  • Expecting StateFlow.collectAsState() to be "free": it adds a collector and sets a state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does Snapshot.withMutableSnapshot do? → Batches writes and applies atomically; all or nothing.
  2. neverEqualPolicy? → Always notifies, used when mutating in place.
  3. What is a write conflict? → Two mutable snapshots modify the same state record; apply fails unless a merge policy resolves (verify details per runtime).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior explains versioned records, observers, and equality policy and relates it to storms.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Feed list not updating because a MutableList was mutated in place inside mutableStateOf.

questions.contextHtml:
Release 5.14 shipped to 25% and the on-call alert fired: ANR rate 0.4% -> 2.1% and battery drain complaints on the "Offers" screen. Traces show the main thread at 100% in Recomposer.runRecomposeAndApplyChanges; Perfetto shows recomposition slices back to back across frames, 0 idle. Layout Inspector shows OfferBanner recomposition count rising at 60/s with no user interaction. Diff in 5.14 added the following:

@Composable
fun OfferBanner(vm: OffersVM) {
    var shown by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
    val offers by vm.offers.collectAsState()
    shown = offers.size           // "keep count in sync"
    Text("Showing $shown of ${offers.size}")
}

The network layer was also changed in the same release (red herring).
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: cause, fix, and what process changes you propose.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back the network change." Wrong correlation; ignores the main-thread recomposition evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the loop persist with no data change? Is only 5.14 affected? Does it reproduce in a debug composable test?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout, remote-disable the banner, or ship a hotfix; roll back is the safest.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) state write in composition after read, (b) collectAsState emitting repeatedly (flow re-emits equal list), (c) network retries, (d) animation loop.
  4. How I'd verify: Perfetto shows continuous recompose; add SideEffect logging; write a ComposeTestRule that fails on more than N recompositions; compiler/Layout Inspector counts.
  5. Root cause: Writing shown in the body after it was read in the same body invalidates the scope again; if the written value is the same, structural equality prevents a notify, so the loop needs a change. Here offers.size equal once settled, so a second loop source exists: vm.offers re-emitting a new list instance each poll (equal contents but StateFlow equality...). Verify: a flow emitting a new List per poll with equal contents does not re-emit on StateFlow, but a SharedFlow/flow{} would, so the write loop stays alive via repeated collectAsState sets. Either way, the body write is the bug.
  6. Fix: Delete shown; derive val shown = offers.size. If a derived state is needed, derivedStateOf. If a one-time sync is needed, use an effect.
  7. Prevention: Test asserting max recompositions; staged rollout gates on ANR; review rule "no state writes in composition"; consider Compose lint for backwards writes (verify availability).
  8. Trade-offs: Rolling back vs hotfix: rollback is faster; hotfix keeps other improvements. Do not paper over with Dispatchers changes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did the ANR appear only on low-end devices? → Main thread saturation; high-end frames absorb loops better.
  • How would StrictMode help? → It would not; use trace/test.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "sync two states" helper turned into a 60 Hz recomposition loop during a holiday campaign; the rollout gate caught it at 25%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames network.
  • Hire: finds the write-in-body and removes derived state.
  • Strong hire: explains snapshot invalidation, equality policy, tests, rollout gates and reviews.

questions.contextHtml: A PM pings you: "Compose made our Settings screen slow. Fix it by tomorrow." That is all you have. The screen has ~40 rows (toggles, text, dividers). Dev builds on the PM's phone feel laggy when opening it; Play vitals show no jank regression on this screen and a cold-start p95 of 2.6 s overall. Someone suggests "just replace it with XML".
questions.promptHtml: How do you handle this?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts rewriting or adds remember everywhere without measuring.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Slow when? Opening the screen, scrolling, or toggling? Which build and device? Compared to what baseline? Is it new since a release (bisect)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed from field data; first reproduce on a release-like build.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) debug build without R8/baseline profiles (very likely), (b) first-composition class loading, (c) real over-recomposition from a state read, (d) heavy Material components or images.
  4. How I'd verify: Run release build (or benchmark variant) with Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric + StartupTimingMetric; Layout Inspector recomposition counts; compose compiler reports; Perfetto.
  5. Root cause: To be determined; most likely debug-build overhead, which is not a user problem.
  6. Fix: If release numbers are fine, close with the evidence; if not, fix the concrete finding (deferred read, keys, baseline profile).
  7. Prevention: Make the benchmark a CI job; document "judge perf on release+profile".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No XML rewrite; it throws away shared design system and fixes nothing if the cause is a debug build.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if release is slow only on a 2 GB device? → Profile there; check memory pressure, image sizes, and composition depth.
  • What if PM insists? → Share the traces, and offer a before/after number.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "Compose is slow" claim was a debug build with the layout inspector attached; the release build ran at 120 fps.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: starts changing code or rewriting.
  • Hire: asks clarifying questions and measures release.
  • Strong hire: separates debug from release, uses Macrobenchmark and field data, communicates results to the PM.
